action.description: Dummy root representing the unselected initial design state.
action.rationale: A benchmark result and execution-family choice are required before specializing the implementation.

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: H100 strongly favors tensor-core-compatible convolution tiles. The 256 input and output channels align well with tensor-core dimensions, while implicit 3x3 patch addressing and NCHW output layout complicate operand formation.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Each convolution performs approximately 4608 floating-point operations per output element, so the two convolutions dominate GroupNorm, SiLU, and residual arithmetic. A tensor-core path can be compute-bound; a scalar-FMA path is likely instruction- or compute-bound.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: FP32 reference semantics and the tight relative tolerance may restrict TF32 use, removing much of H100's tensor-core advantage.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Weights are about 2.25 MiB per convolution and are highly reusable. Activations range from tens of MiB to roughly 1 GiB per tensor; materializing convolution and normalization intermediates creates substantial HBM traffic at the largest spatial sizes.
memory_bandwidth.risk: The mandatory global GroupNorm reductions prevent straightforward end-to-end fusion and can force multiple full activation reads and writes.

register_pressure.notes: Convolution accumulators, masked halo handling, and GroupNorm statistics all compete for registers. Keeping a complete GroupNorm domain resident is infeasible for most shapes, so staging is expected.
register_pressure.risk: Aggressive output tiling or attempted convolution-normalization fusion can reduce occupancy through accumulator and shared-memory growth.

nodes.notes: The first passing implementation establishes a 1.027x end-to-end baseline improvement across all 20 workloads. The result validates staged execution as a practical starting point, but it does not yet distinguish the proposed Triton ownership families because convolution and normalization remain delegated to PyTorch ATen.

action.description: Implement a correctness-first staged pipeline with tensor-core-oriented implicit-GEMM convolutions, materialized convolution outputs, standalone GroupNorm reductions, and fused GN-affine-SiLU stores; fuse residual addition into the final normalization store.
action.rationale: This family best matches the fixed 256x2304 convolution dimensions and provides a robust baseline across all listed shapes while isolating numerical and tiling issues.
action.title: Build the implicit-GEMM staged baseline

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: M can represent N*H*W positions, N is 256 output channels, and K is 256*3*3=2304. N and K are favorable tensor-core multiples, but constructing A requires masked NCHW patch gathers and B requires a compatible interpretation of OIHW weights.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: cuDNN/ATen convolution maps the dominant 256-channel compute well to H100; measured end-to-end performance is 1.053x baseline.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The two convolution outputs remain materialized, but the staged pipeline is consistently viable across all 20 workloads.

register_pressure.notes: ATen owns convolution and normalization reductions, while the elementwise Triton kernel has modest live state.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: This family uses optimized library convolutions, materialized native GroupNorm operations, and a small Triton SiLU/residual epilogue. It is the only family with passing end-to-end evidence across all 20 workloads.
bottleneck: convolution compute for large feature maps, plus synchronization and memory traffic between staged operators.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The latest child preserved correctness and measured a 1.052997x baseline factor, strengthening the staged implicit-GEMM family as the practical foundation. The gain is modest, so further progress depends on removing a materialization boundary rather than only tuning the elementwise launch.
next bet: Retain the library convolution path and replace native GroupNorm output materialization with explicit statistics plus a fused Triton normalization epilogue.

action.description: Prototype convolution kernels that emit output values and per-tile sum and sum-of-squares partials, followed by compact per-group reduction and normalization-activation kernels; include the residual in the second stage's final store.
action.rationale: Generating GroupNorm statistics while convolution accumulators are already live can remove the separate statistics scan over each convolution output, which is most valuable for very large activation tensors.
action.title: Prototype convolution-produced GroupNorm statistics

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: Convolution tiles must align output-channel ownership with 8-channel GroupNorm boundaries or emit separately addressable group partials. H100 has ample compute, but cross-program statistics still require a global completion boundary.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The approach can retain tensor-core convolution throughput, but cross-program statistic reduction and a later normalized store remain synchronization challenges.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Producing normalization statistics alongside convolution tiles could avoid a separate full activation read, which is most relevant for the largest spatial workloads.

register_pressure.notes: Maintaining convolution accumulators and partial sum/sumsq state together can materially reduce occupancy or force spills.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: This family remains unimplemented; the passing evidence comes from an ATen-materialized pipeline.
bottleneck: expected synchronization and reduction complexity, with register pressure as the primary implementation risk.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
what changed after eval_result: The staged baseline is already slightly faster than reference, but it confirms that full intermediate materialization remains in the execution path. Produced statistics still has upside on very large H*W, although the modest total normalization share lowers confidence in a large end-to-end gain.
next bet: Defer until the lower-risk fused GroupNorm epilogue quantifies how much normalization traffic matters; pursue this family only if large-spatial workloads remain bandwidth-sensitive.
SELF_CHECK: This family streams or reduces statistics as convolution tiles are produced, excluding both fully materialized normalization and complete-group resident execution.

action.description: Prototype a small-shape path where each program owns one or a small number of complete output groups for a convolution stage, reduces GroupNorm statistics locally, applies affine and SiLU, and writes only the activated stage output.
action.rationale: At H=W=64, one GroupNorm domain contains 32768 values, making resident or chunk-looped group ownership marginally plausible and potentially eliminating pre-normalization global materialization and extra launches.
action.title: Prototype group-resident normalization

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: A 64x64 group has 8 output channels and 32768 FP32 values, or 128 KiB before overhead. This approaches practical per-CTA shared-memory limits and limits blocks per SM. Larger spatial sizes are not resident candidates.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The ownership model is plausible only for the smallest domains and may sacrifice convolution parallelism or occupancy on H100.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Keeping a normalization group resident can reduce intermediate traffic for small spatial domains, but the benefit narrows as the group domain grows.

register_pressure.notes: A complete 8-channel group over even 64x64 spatial positions is too large for registers, requiring shared-memory staging, decomposition, or multiple passes.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: This family remains unimplemented; no group-resident convolution or normalization kernel was exercised by the passing solution.
bottleneck: capacity, occupancy, and synchronization rather than raw arithmetic throughput.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
what changed after eval_result: A conventional staged path already reaches 1.027386x across all workloads, reducing the value of a narrow small-domain specialization. The broad 64..1024 spatial range makes a complete-group ownership strategy less generally applicable.
next bet: Keep this as a lower-priority specialization for B-small, 64x64 cases only after per-workload profiling demonstrates a meaningful gap that the staged GroupNorm epilogue cannot close.
SELF_CHECK: This family assigns complete normalization-group domains to resident execution and excludes both materialized full-tensor staging and convolution-produced distributed statistics.

action.title: Fuse GroupNorm affine, SiLU, and residual stores

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: This remains a sound staging point, but the child custom-reduction implementation now dominates it with a measured 1.0927x baseline factor.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The successful child confirms that eliminating standalone affine, activation, and residual passes is valuable, while further gains require improving the reduction itself.

register_pressure.notes: The epilogue fusion has modest scalar state and did not introduce observed correctness or compilation failures across the workload set.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
- does: Uses two torch conv2d calls and two ATen native_group_norm calls. Triton performs in-place SiLU after each normalization and also folds the residual addition into the second SiLU kernel.
- bottleneck: bandwidth and launch/synchronization overhead from materialized normalization outputs and separate ATen-to-Triton stages.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: no
- if_no: The intended action was to own GroupNorm affine, SiLU, and output storage in one Triton normalization epilogue. The implementation leaves reduction and affine application inside native_group_norm and only fuses SiLU plus the optional residual add afterward.
UPDATE_BELIEF:
- All 20 workloads passed at 4.962 ms and 1.053x baseline, close to the predicted 1.06x, confirming that the lightweight in-place epilogue is useful but modest.
- next bet: Replace native_group_norm with a Triton group-per-program reduction that applies affine, SiLU, and optional residual during its final store; this directly removes the remaining normalization-to-epilogue materialization and launch.

action.title: Use custom GroupNorm reduction with fused SiLU and residual epilogue

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: ATen convolution retains cuDNN tensor-core selection while Triton handles the bandwidth-oriented normalization epilogues.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The custom epilogue avoids separate affine, SiLU, and residual-add tensor passes. GroupNorm still reads convolution output twice for statistics and normalization.

register_pressure.notes: The 2048-element reduction block and paired aligned-path accumulators increase per-program register demand, but all 20 workloads pass on H100.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: The solution uses ATen Conv3x3 for both convolutions and custom Triton GroupNorm kernels that fuse affine, SiLU, and the final residual addition. Large low-batch spatial workloads use native GroupNorm, while aligned custom reductions process two 2048-element blocks per loop.
bottleneck: compute, with the two dense 256-channel convolutions dominant and GroupNorm reduction latency and bandwidth secondary.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The attached pipeline passed all 20 workloads and reached 1.1577x mean speedup, confirming that custom fused normalization is compatible with the numerical tolerance and beneficial across the evaluated range. The hybrid native/custom dispatch also indicates that one reduction strategy is not optimal for every spatial extent.
next bet: Refine the native GroupNorm dispatch for very long per-group reductions, where a single Triton program performs many serial block iterations. This is a small host-side specialization with limited correctness risk.

action.title: Continue with the fused custom GroupNorm pipeline

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The measured 1.1577x factor remains the best result; H100 utilization is still principally determined by the two ATen convolutions.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The fused GroupNorm, SiLU, and residual stores remain advantageous for the majority of evaluated shapes by avoiding additional full-tensor passes.

register_pressure.notes: The 2048-element reduction block and loop-carried accumulators are acceptable on covered shapes, but long reductions remain sensitive to occupancy and serialization.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: The implementation adds a mask-free paired-block path when the spatial extent aligns to 2048 elements and dispatches large low-batch tensors to native GroupNorm. The final custom path fuses normalization, affine, SiLU, and residual addition into one store pass.
bottleneck: compute overall; within the changed code, long serial GroupNorm reductions are the main latency and synchronization concern.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The solution passed 20 of 20 workloads at 4.1723 ms and achieved a 1.1577x mean speedup over baseline. This raises confidence that workload-aware GroupNorm specialization is effective without compromising correctness.
next bet: Extend the native/custom dispatch decision to all very large per-group reductions rather than restricting it to batch sizes at most two. This directly targets serial reduction depth while leaving the proven convolution path unchanged.

action.title: Dispatch native GroupNorm for long reductions

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The full passing workload set confirms that native normalization is a sound fallback for large spatial reductions on H100.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The dispatch pays native intermediate traffic only where the custom single-program reduction would repeatedly stream very large groups.

register_pressure.notes: Long reductions avoid the custom kernel's large loop and paired accumulator pressure.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:

- bottleneck: synchronization and insufficient parallelism inside very long per-group reductions, with convolution compute dominating end-to-end time.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
- what changed after eval_result?: All 20 workloads passed and the complete pipeline reached a 1.1577x mean speedup, increasing confidence that the long-reduction dispatch boundary is robust.
- next bet: Preserve the large-map thresholds and tune only the low-batch boundary, where the custom kernel launches too few group programs for H100 occupancy.

register_pressure.notes: The 4096-element reduction block and paired accumulators increase per-program register demand, but the evaluated implementation passed all 20 workloads.

action.title: Continue with workload-aware GroupNorm dispatch

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Both convolutions remain on optimized ATen/cuDNN paths, and H100 executes only the normalization and pointwise epilogues in Triton. All 20 workloads passed at 1.1577x mean baseline performance.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The conditional custom GroupNorm epilogues avoid separate affine and SiLU traffic on smaller feature maps, while native GroupNorm is retained where long serial reductions would reread too much data.

register_pressure.notes: The 4096-element reduction block and paired accumulators increase per-program register demand, but the evaluated dispatch avoids the worst long-reduction cases.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
- does: The solution runs both 3x3 convolutions through ATen, uses a fused Triton GroupNorm-affine-SiLU kernel on shorter reductions, and dispatches long reductions to native GroupNorm. The second custom epilogue also fuses the residual addition; the native path uses a fused Triton SiLU-plus-residual pointwise kernel.
- bottleneck: compute, dominated by the two dense 256-channel 3x3 convolutions; normalization synchronization and launch overhead remain secondary bottlenecks.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
- what changed after eval_result?: The candidate passed all 20 workloads with 4.1321 ms mean latency and a 1.1577x speedup over baseline. This confirms that conservative shape-dependent native/custom GroupNorm dispatch preserves numerical correctness and remains beneficial across the evaluated range.
- next bet: Lower only the low-batch native GroupNorm spatial threshold to cover occupancy-poor custom reductions such as batch-one 64x64 maps. This is a narrowly scoped dispatch change that can improve latency without disturbing the high-batch cases where the custom fused epilogue has enough parallel groups.

action.title: Extend native GroupNorm dispatch for low-batch maps

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: All workloads passed, and the refined stage-specific descendant demonstrates that batch and spatial dimensions are useful H100 dispatch signals.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The descendant result confirms that batch-aware native/custom selection reduces normalization overhead across the evaluated shape range.

register_pressure.notes: Fixed large-block custom reductions remain a pressure risk, but low-batch dispatch prevents their use on several unfavorable long reductions.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: This path introduced batch-aware GroupNorm dispatch and is now refined by separate stage-1 and stage-2 thresholds. Convolutions remain cuDNN operations while custom Triton kernels own favorable normalization epilogues.
bottleneck: compute, dominated by the two 256-channel 3x3 convolutions; normalization launch and reduction costs remain secondary.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The passing stage-specific descendant at 1.1766x strengthens the original belief that low-batch shapes require distinct native/custom crossover points. It also shows that one shared threshold was leaving measurable performance available.
next bet: Continue below the stage-specific node with launch-configuration tuning rather than adding another dispatch sibling.

action.title: Dispatch GroupNorm independently for each residual stage

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: cuDNN continues to own both dense 3x3 convolutions on H100, while stage-specific normalization dispatch avoids forcing one reduction strategy across dissimilar tensor sizes.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The custom paths fuse affine, SiLU, and the stage-two residual addition into the normalization write, while native GroupNorm is retained only where its long-reduction implementation wins.

register_pressure.notes: The 4096-element Triton reduction and dual accumulators are substantial but confined to spatial regimes where the custom kernel remains competitive.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: The solution runs both 3x3 convolutions through PyTorch/cuDNN and independently dispatches each GroupNorm stage between a fused Triton reduction/epilogue and native GroupNorm. Stage two additionally fuses SiLU with the residual add in either the Triton normalization kernel or a dedicated pointwise kernel.
bottleneck: compute, dominated by the two dense 256x256 3x3 convolutions; normalization synchronization and memory traffic remain the main adjustable secondary cost.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The complete 20-workload pass at 4.1944 ms and 1.1541x mean baseline speedup provides strong evidence that independent stage dispatch is robust and that the numerical behavior is within tolerance. The result also confirms that retaining native GroupNorm for long reductions is preferable to applying the custom one-program-per-group kernel universally.
next bet: Refine the coarse batch <= 2 versus batch > 2 thresholds into a small number of batch buckets, especially for stage two. This can reduce normalization latency near the current boundaries without changing convolution ownership or numerical behavior.

action.title: Target the normalization dispatch bottleneck

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The implementation preserves vendor convolution kernels and applies Triton only to bandwidth- and synchronization-sensitive normalization epilogues.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Fused custom epilogues eliminate separate SiLU and residual traffic on selected shapes; native paths trade that traffic for faster long reductions.

register_pressure.notes: Large Triton reduction blocks increase register demand, but threshold dispatch limits exposure to unfavorable long-reduction shapes.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: The current solution uses cuDNN convolutions plus stage-specific native-versus-Triton GroupNorm dispatch. The Triton paths fuse affine, SiLU, and, for stage two, residual addition into the normalization store.
bottleneck: compute for the convolutions, with normalization reduction synchronization and intermediate memory traffic as the primary optimization surface available to a small refinement.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The candidate passed all 20 workloads at 4.1944 ms, achieving a measured 1.1541x mean speedup over baseline. This raises confidence that the dispatch and fused epilogues improve aggregate performance without shape-specific correctness regressions.
next bet: Calibrate separate native GroupNorm thresholds for a few batch-size buckets and for each stage. The current binary low-batch rule likely leaves modest latency near threshold boundaries, while a dispatch-only change has low implementation and correctness risk.

action.title: Dispatch native and custom GroupNorm by stage, batch, and spatial size

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The stage-specific thresholds fit H100 behavior well enough to pass all 20 workloads at 1.1624x mean speedup.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The dispatch preserves fused affine, SiLU, and residual stores where custom GroupNorm is favorable while using the native implementation for long reductions.

register_pressure.notes: Custom reductions retain large live accumulators, but dispatch limits their use on spatial sizes where that pressure is most costly.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
does: The solution materializes both convolutions with ATen, then dispatches each GroupNorm stage between native PyTorch and a Triton fused GroupNorm-SiLU epilogue using batch- and spatial-size thresholds. Stage two fuses the residual addition into either the custom GroupNorm kernel or a separate Triton SiLU-residual kernel after native GroupNorm.
bottleneck: compute for the two dense 3x3 convolutions, with reduction synchronization, launch latency, and memory traffic from materialized intermediates as secondary costs.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The passing 20/20 result and 1.1624x mean speedup strengthen the case for shape- and stage-dependent GroupNorm dispatch. The remaining opportunity inside this family is incremental because convolution compute dominates total latency.
next bet: Continue with a child refinement that changes the custom GroupNorm reduction block size by spatial bucket, preserving the validated native/custom thresholds while reducing excess lane work and register pressure for small maps.

action.title: Tune custom GroupNorm launch configuration by spatial bucket

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: The broad workload pass validates the bucket strategy, while the small prediction gap indicates configuration tuning remains workload-sensitive.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Launch bucketing preserves the fused memory behavior, but it does not by itself reduce the dominant tensor traffic.

register_pressure.notes: Different launch configurations can improve occupancy, but overly large warp counts may increase register pressure.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:

- bottleneck: latency and synchronization for small reductions; bandwidth remains material for large tensors.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The latest passed evaluation strengthens confidence that launch and spatial bucketing is directionally correct, but the observed 1.1588x speedup is below the 1.17x estimate. The next refinement should preserve the bucket ownership decision while tuning warp and stage configuration within each bucket.
Next bet: evaluate a small set of composable warp/stage configurations under the active block-size refinement rather than creating a competing baseline variant.

action.title: Tune custom GroupNorm block size by spatial bucket

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Observed performance on H100 is strong across all 20 workloads, and spatial block selection is aligned with the variable spatial-size distribution.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The custom path performs in-place normalization, affine, SiLU, and residual stores, reducing intermediate traffic; remaining convolution and normalization loads keep bandwidth relevant.

register_pressure.notes: The aligned two-block reduction and fused epilogue improve reuse but increase live reduction state and address calculations.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:

The surrounding implementation keeps convolution in ATen while fusing GroupNorm affine, SiLU, and residual work in Triton.
- bottleneck: bandwidth and latency, with kernel launch and synchronization overhead remaining important for small spatial workloads.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
- aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
The passed result confirms that spatial block-size bucketing is beneficial: 4.1573 ms mean latency versus 4.4572 ms reference, a 1.1588x speedup across all 20 workloads. The result is slightly below the 1.17x prediction, so block size is helping but is not the only remaining limiter.
Next bet: tune warps and stages jointly with the existing 2048/4096 block buckets, especially for small and irregular spatial sizes. This should target launch latency and reduction occupancy without changing the proven computation path.
PERF_GAP: expected_vs_observed=1.17x_vs_1.1588x; hypothesized_reason=the fixed num_warps and num_stages choices leave occupancy and launch-latency gains on the table for some spatial buckets.

register_pressure.notes: The paired accumulators and compile-time unrolled block loops are viable on H100, though 4096-element blocks with eight warps can reduce occupancy in some buckets.

nodes.notes:

action.title: Tune the fused stage-two GroupNorm block for 64x64 high-batch workloads

action.title: Tune the fused stage-one GroupNorm block for 64x64 high-batch workloads

kernel_summary: This is a mixed dense 3x3 convolution, per-group reduction, nonlinear activation, and residual kernel with two global normalization barriers. The fixed C=256 and convolution reduction K=2304 are favorable for H100 tensor-core tiling, while NCHW patch formation, zero-padded boundaries, and FP32 accuracy requirements are the main compute risks. GroupNorm independently reduces 8*H*W values for each of B*32 groups, preventing ordinary single-launch end-to-end fusion; a practical first design should use staged convolutions and fuse affine, SiLU, and residual work around the mandatory phase boundaries. Large spatial workloads may be sensitive to activation materialization, large-batch 64x64 workloads should favor convolution throughput, and small-batch 64x64 workloads may instead be limited by launch latency and available group-level parallelism.

May temporary workspace tensors be allocated or cached between calls, and are convolution weights reused across invocations in a way that permits preprocessing?
